clue.text: Put on guard from a combination of fear and wonder

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are mixed together into one new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone is alarmed by a mixture of fright and amazement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a combination of' tells you to mix the letters of FEAR and WONDER together.
explanation.definitionFit: To forewarn is to alert in advance, so someone put on guard has been cautioned beforehand.

clue.text: Taking the middle course is for us

indicators.note: only the central letters of the word course are kept, dropping its first and last

explanation.surface: Choosing the moderate path is the right policy for our group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking the middle' keeps OURS, course without its first and last letters; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something meant for us belongs to us, which is the possessive pronoun.

clue.text: Company guard

explanation.surface: A firm that provides security staff.
explanation.definitionFit: An escort is a companion who keeps someone company, and also a protective guard travelling alongside.

clue.text: A classical way to gain height as a flier

indicators.note: the preceding pieces take on the next one, which is added after them

parts.note: via is Latin for road or way, the language of the classical world
a tor is a rocky hill or peak, especially on Dartmoor in England

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned method of climbing in the world of a pilot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'classical' points to Latin, where VIA means way; a TOR is a high rocky hill in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: An aviator is a pilot, someone who flies aircraft.

clue.text: Women prepared to follow orders

parts.note: reads as obedient women, but orders are religious communities whose female members take vows

explanation.surface: Women who are ready to obey commands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'orders' looks like commands; here it means religious orders.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of a female religious community take vows and belong to an order.

clue.text: Hangs around with a number of friends

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for five hundred
allies are friends who side with you

explanation.surface: Someone loiters in the company of several mates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link. D is 500 in Roman numerals, a common crossword way to clue a number.
explanation.definitionFit: To dally is to dawdle or linger idly, wasting time.

clue.text: Located the cause of the trouble and criticised

definitions.text: Located the cause of the trouble

explanation.surface: Someone diagnosed what went wrong and complained about it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally means discovered the defect, and idiomatically means complained or carped.

clue.text: Vicar heart-broken to see arch moulding

indicators.note: broken means the letters of vicar and heart are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: A clergyman is devastated by the sight of a curved decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heart-broken' looks like the vicar's emotion, but 'broken' is the anagram signal working on VICAR plus HEART; 'to see' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An architrave is the moulded frame around a doorway or arch, or the beam resting on columns.

clue.text: Trip to the city

parts.note: Ur is the ancient Mesopotamian city, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A journey into town.
explanation.walkthrough: UR, the Sumerian city, is crossword shorthand for 'city'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tour is a journey or excursion visiting places.

clue.text: Part of trial can collapse

indicators.note: collapse means these words fall down and are rebuilt in a different order

explanation.surface: Some of the court case might fall apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collapse' rearranges OF TRIAL CAN, so 'of' is fodder rather than a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Fractional means being only a portion or a small piece of a whole.

clue.text: Craft project

explanation.surface: A piece of handiwork done as a school assignment.
explanation.definitionFit: A launch is a motor boat, a vessel; to launch is to propel or hurl something forward.

clue.text: Troops are also part of the scheme

indicators.note: the word for also becomes a piece set within the word for the scheme

parts.note: a scheme is a plan
too means also

explanation.surface: Soldiers are included in the strategy as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part of' puts TOO inside PLAN; 'are' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A platoon is a small military unit of soldiers.

clue.text: Good story about a fellow can be forgiven

indicators.note: the word for good story goes around the word for a fellow

parts.note: a parable is a story told to teach a moral lesson
a don is a fellow of a university college

explanation.surface: A fine tale about some man may be excused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps PARABLE around DON; a DON is a fellow at Oxford or Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pardonable is excusable, able to be overlooked.

clue.text: He dispensed with scruples some time ago

definitions.text: He dispensed with scruples some time ago

parts.words: He dispensed with scruples some time ago
parts.note: reads as a man who abandoned his morals, but a scruple was an old unit of weight used when making up medicines

explanation.surface: A man who abandoned his conscience long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dispensed with' suggests got rid of; here it means made up prescriptions, measured in scruples, a small apothecaries' weight.
explanation.definitionFit: An apothecary was a historical pharmacist who prepared and sold medicines.

clue.text: No more old army slang from Poona?

indicators.note: the question mark lets the word from suggest the letters of Poona are made into something new

explanation.surface: Soldiers' jargon for finished, perhaps originating in an Indian city.
explanation.walkthrough: Poona (now Pune) was an Indian garrison town; the word actually comes from the French il n'y en a plus, so the '?' admits the false origin.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoo was First World War soldiers' slang for finished, done for, gone.

clue.text: Profit from a charity performance

explanation.surface: Earnings made at a fundraising show.
explanation.definitionFit: A benefit is an advantage or gain, and also a show staged to raise money for a cause.

clue.text: Live down under

parts.note: to be is to exist or live
low means down, as in feeling low

explanation.surface: Residing in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down under' reads as Australia, but 'down' gives LOW and 'under' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Below and under both mean beneath, lower in position.

clue.text: Is violent and ruins the gears

indicators.note: ruins means the word gears is wrecked and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A driver behaves aggressively and wrecks the gearbox.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruins' scrambles GEARS; 'and' and 'the' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: To rage is to act with fury or storm violently.

clue.text: Castle in the air?

parts.note: reads as a daydream, but a chess castle shares its name with a black bird that flies

explanation.surface: An impossible dream or fantasy.
explanation.walkthrough: A castle in the air is an idle dream; the chess piece also called a castle has the same name as a crow-like bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The chess castle and the crow-family bird share one name.

clue.text: Novice reporter goes to a Caribbean island

parts.note: a cub is a young, inexperienced journalist

explanation.surface: A trainee journalist travels to the West Indies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean Sea.

clue.text: Seek to attack

explanation.surface: A plan to go looking for a fight.
explanation.definitionFit: To go for something is to try to obtain it; to go for someone is to assault them.

clue.text: It's difficult to see if they're broken

definitions.text: It's difficult to see if they're broken

parts.words: It's difficult to see if they're broken
parts.note: reads as damage being hard to spot, but means you struggle to see when your spectacles are smashed

explanation.surface: Damage that is hard to notice.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue seems to say the breakage is hard to detect; in fact a broken pair leaves the wearer unable to see well.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectacles help the wearer see, so vision suffers when they are smashed.

clue.text: Stalks out of the stage crowd

explanation.surface: Someone creeps away from the actors gathered on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Actors playing a background crowd traditionally mutter the word to sound like chatter.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhubarb is a plant eaten for its pink stalks, and the word extras murmur to fake background conversation.

clue.text: Moorish gentleman to run rings round the students

indicators.note: the two ring shapes go around the remaining pieces

parts.note: two rings are two letter Os, round in shape
L is a learner driver's plate, so students gives two Ls

explanation.surface: A man from North Africa outpaces the undergraduates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'run rings round' means outclass, but here 'round' puts OO around THE plus LL; 'to run' is a link. L for learner is from British learner-driver plates.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragic hero is the Moor of Venice.

clue.text: Sound cheerful while going round the short way

indicators.note: the word while encircles the abbreviation for street

parts.note: St is the short form of street, a way

explanation.surface: Being merry while taking a shortcut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the short way' suggests a shortcut but means ST, the abbreviation of street; 'going round' puts WHILE around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Whistling a tune is a classic sign of a happy mood.

clue.text: Drawing-room at Broadcasting House?

parts.note: a drawing-room is a parlour, but read as a room for drawing it is an artist's workplace, and the BBC headquarters has rooms for broadcasting

explanation.surface: A parlour inside the BBC's London headquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: Broadcasting House is the BBC's London headquarters, full of recording rooms; an artist's workroom is a room for drawing.
explanation.definitionFit: Artists work in one and broadcasters record in one.

clue.text: Awkward cases caught in a doorway?

indicators.note: the abbreviation for caught is placed inside the jumbled letters
awkward suggests the letters of cases are clumsily jumbled

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Clumsy boxes are stuck in an entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awkward' jumbles CASES to ACESS; 'in' puts C inside. C for caught comes from cricket scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: Access is a way in, an entrance, which a doorway provides.

clue.text: How Beethoven finished a set of four notes

explanation.surface: The way the composer ended a sequence of musical notes.
explanation.walkthrough: Beethoven lost his hearing late in life. The second reading spells four musical notes: D, E, A, F.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven ended his life unable to hear, and the four letters are each the names of musical notes.

clue.text: Man, for example, spreading lies

indicators.note: spreading means the letters of lies are spread out and reordered

explanation.surface: Some fellow telling untruths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like a person, but it is the Isle of Man, an island between Britain and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is an example of an island.

clue.text: She may provide flying courses

parts.note: reads as an instructor teaching pilots, but courses are meal courses served in the air

explanation.surface: A woman who teaches lessons in aviation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'courses' suggests training; here it means the meal courses served aboard an aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabin attendant serves meals to passengers during a flight.

clue.text: An ornithological frolic

parts.note: a word meaning a bit of fun that is also the name of a songbird

explanation.surface: A bird-watchers' outing for fun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a songbird and a carefree spree or prank.

clue.text: Secure telephone for the cracksman

parts.note: safe means secure
blower is British slang for the telephone

explanation.surface: A protected phone line for a burglar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for the' is a link. 'The blower' is old British slang for the phone.
explanation.definitionFit: A cracksman is a burglar, especially one who breaks open strongboxes with explosives.
